Iran Steps Up Hormuz Tanker Attacks as Oil Prices Slide
Iran has intensified attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz in recent weeks, just as crude oil flows from the Persian Gulf recover and oil prices fall amid expectations of oversupply within months.
The number of attacks soared in October to the highest level since the Iran war began at the end of February, and has continued at nearly daily occurrences so far in November, according to data compiled by Bloomberg .
Meanwhile, crude oil volumes flowing from the Strait of Hormuz have declined in recent days, although it's unclear if this is entirely due to the more frequent attacks on tankers.
"Security risks continue to weigh on tanker operations in the Gulf," Maria Bertzeletou, Senior Market Analyst at Signal Group, wrote in an analysis this week.
"Repeated attacks continue to restrict the pool of owners willing to accept Gulf employment, while elevated war-risk insurance costs and operational delays add to voyage expenses and limit effective vessel availability."
So far this month, Iran has been reporting nearly daily incidents of tankers hitting naval mines in corridors that Iran has designated as "unauthorized" in the Strait of Hormuz.
Non-Iranian observers and organizations also report more frequent attacks on tankers in and near the Strait of Hormuz.
Five tankers were struck near Hormuz in the week between November 11 and 18, according to remote-sensing intelligence by Windward .
"This highlights Iran's continued strategy of maritime attrition, and it is unlikely to ease unless diplomatic conditions change," the maritime intelligence firm said on Wednesday.
ADNOC Logistics & Services, a unit of Abu Dhabi's national oil company ADNOC, confirmed that one of its vessels was attacked while transiting the Strait of Hormuz on the evening of November 17.
The number of attacks could be even higher, as not all incidents are being reported to the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) and the International Maritime Organization (IMO).

items.title: Poland accuses Russia of "intentional provocation" as missiles hit NATO soil, kill at least 8 in Ukraine - CBS News
items.summary: Poland accuses Russia of "intentional provocation" as missiles hit NATO soil, kill at least 8 in Ukraine  CBS News
items.content:
Poland's government said Russian missiles landed in the country overnight as Vladimir Putin's forces hammered Ukraine with what President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called "one of the largest attacks" since the war began. The strikes on Ukraine killed at least eight people, according to Zelenskyy.
The prime minister of Poland, a NATO member, decried the Russian weapons landing in his country as "an intentional provocation" of the U.S.-led military alliance.
"We know that what landed on Polish soil came from Russia. Therefore — ⁠and this is not just my own assessment, but ‌also that of our foreign partners, including those within NATO — it does not look like an ‌accident," Prime Minister ⁠Donald Tusk said. "It ‌appears that we ⁠are dealing with an intentional ⁠provocation."
Members of the Polish military gather near the site where an object fell, in Rudnik and Sanem, Poland, November 20, 2026. Polish authorities said they investigate at least three objects found near the border with Ukraine on Friday.
"Russia is trying to compensate for its military and diplomatic impotence with precisely this kind of terror," Zelenskyy wrote, adding that Putin's attempt to "redraw the world" with his Chinese and U.S. counterparts during their summit Thursday in China had been a "failure."
Russia fired more than 400 drones and 110 missiles at Ukraine overnight and early Friday, including cluster munitions, Zelenskyy said in a fiery social media post . Some of the Russian weapons hit the Austrian embassy and landed near the Netherlands embassy in Kyiv, prompting France to call for a meeting of the United Nations Security Council.
"Russia will have to answer for this," French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot wrote in a social media post.
Poland's defense minister said three Russian weapons, believed to have been two missiles and a drone, entered southeast Poland's airspace on Friday. Poland scrambled fighter jets and Patriot anti-missile systems in the country's southeast were activated, but no injuries were reported.
Drones have repeatedly entered the airspace of Poland and other NATO countries, mostly near Ukraine but not all, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022.
The Article 5 collective defense clause in NATO's founding charter states that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all 32.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said in a Friday social media post that he had spoken with Tusk "about the grave violations of Polish airspace overnight" and stressed that the alliance stands "in solidarity with Poland and will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend."
"This incident is clearly dangerous — a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," Rutte said. "I condemn Russia's attacks as well as its ongoing war. We continue to stand united as Allies and will continue to support Ukraine."
NATO's Supreme Allied Commander for Europe, U.S. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, was in "close contact with Poland's chief of defense and minister of defense as Poland's investigation into the overnight airspace violations continues," his spokesperson Martin O'Donnell told CBS News on Friday.
Members of the Polish Army take part in the Koalicja 26.2 military exercise at the Land Forces Training Range in Nowa Deba, Poland, Nov. 20, 2026.
Thousands of troops from 11 European countries that support Kyiv, members of the so-called Coalition of the Willing , are currently in Poland taking part in a major military exercise framed as training for a possible post-war mission in Ukraine, about 60 miles west of where the Russian weapons landed Friday.
"It is hard to regard it as a coincidence that the time and place of the violation of Polish airspace coincide with the Coalition of the Willing's exercises," Deputy Polish Prime Minister and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote in a social media post .
The escalation comes a day after President Trump sat with Xi and Putin — whom he greeted warmly and called his friend — in Shenzhen, China, for a rare face-to-face meeting that seemed to achieve little .
The presidents discussed the Ukraine war, which Mr. Trump has long pushed to end through negotiations, but soon after the 90-minute meeting, Putin ruled out direct talks with Kyiv , citing a strike earlier this week by Ukrainian forces that severely damaged a highly symbolic bridge linking Russia and Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.
"We will respond to these strikes," Putin warned Thursday. "I want everyone to know this. I believe that our retaliatory actions … will be far more painful than what the Kiev regime did to the bridge."
Ukrainian forces managed to intercept 79 of the 110 missiles Russia launched overnight, Zelenskyy said, but none of the 27 ballistic missiles, which he attributed to Kyiv's lack of interceptors. He has been pleading with the Trump administration to help Ukraine replenish its missile interceptor stocks for months, saying the shortage is being paid for in civilian lives.
Russia's attack targeted Kyiv and nine other regions, leaving more than two dozen people wounded in addition to the eight confirmed to have been killed, according to Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi .
"Missiles hit critical infrastructure in the capital, including bridges," he said. "A water supply facility, office and commercial buildings were damaged."
A man stands amid the debris of an office building that caught fire after it was struck during Russian missile and drone attacks in Kyiv, Ukraine, Nov. 20, 2026.
A hospital in Kharkiv was damaged, as well as businesses in the Mykolaiv, Odesa and Chernihiv regions, and residential buildings in the regions of Dnipropetrovsk, Vinnytsia, Sumy, Chernihiv and Lviv, which is in the far west, close to Poland, Koretskyi said, adding that energy infrastructure was also hit.
Some nuclear plants were forced to reduce power generation after the attacks, according to an energy ministry official .
"The tactics of the strike this time were particularly vile," Zelenskyy said in his post on social media, noting that there had been "several groups of missiles with pauses of 20-30 minutes to complicate extinguishing the fires, clearing the rubble and recovery."
"A clear response from the world to all this is also needed," he said. "It is important that there are not only statements from partners about supporting Ukraine and Ukrainians, but also the implementation of specific agreements on air defense … We very much hope that the Pentagon will release the supply that we expect."

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter.  Subscribe  here to get it delivered to your inbox, and  listen  to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Democrats who won this month's election are looking to use their influence to block funding for the war in Iran before officially taking charge of Congress. President Trump launched attacks last winter without congressional approval, breaking from the tradition of seeking bipartisan support for wars.
Reporters set up for a press conference outside of the U.S. Capitol Building on Nov. 19, 2026, in Washington, D.C.
🎧 Congress must pass a funding measure to avoid a shutdown by Dec. 11. NPR's Claudia Grisales tells Up First that Democrats hold leverage, since their votes are essential for the Republican-controlled Senate to meet the 60-vote threshold. Senate Democrats argue they should use their authority to end what they call an illegal war. Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine aims to include a provision to end war funding in the stopgap bill. Republicans counter that cutting war funding jeopardizes service members in the region. N.C. Republican Sen. Thom Tillis tells Grisales his party may need to explore alternatives if Democrats push for a shutdown. That could include using reconciliation to pass legislation without Democratic votes.
Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping met for the third time this year, underscoring a dilemma for Americans who see China as a business opportunity and a national security risk. Nvidia's former CEO, Jensen Huang, convinced Trump to approve several chip sales before his departure. The House Foreign Affairs Committee yesterday, in a highly unusual step, released a list of requests this year from Nvidia and AMD to sell chips directly to Chinese companies.
🎧 The Trump administration approved the sale of nearly 900,000 advanced chips to Chinese companies as of May 2026. Some of those approvals included well-known firms such as Alibaba and Tencent, which the Pentagon lists as having ties to China's military, NPR's Greg Myre says. During his second term, Trump shifted his stance on China , partly influenced by his relationship with Jinping. The two may meet again next month in Miami.
The U.S. Army has rescheduled the detonation of around 9,500 pounds of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown to Monday, Nov. 23. This decision comes after Iowa lawmakers and two environmental groups pushed for a delay . The plant, which manufactures various types of ammunition, has stored lead azide in a water-ethanol solution in underground tanks for 20 years. Recent inspections found that the tanks were too dry, leading to crystallization and instability. To prevent an accidental explosion, the Army wants to detonate the lead azide under controlled conditions.
🎧 Many Iowans were unaware of the situation until earlier this week , prompting the delay, says Eliza Billingham of NPR network station Iowa Public Radio. Acting Army Secretary Adam R. Telle said on social media that he directed Army Materiel Command to postpone the blasts until the "latest possible moment" before a forecasted drop in temperatures. Army spokesperson Justine Barati previously said that cold weather could make the situation more dangerous. Last month, the Army hosted an informational open house for Middletown residents and shared maps predicting the movement of lead dust . Those maps will need to be revised based on the new forecast, Billingham says. If the detonation proceeds, the Army, EPA and the University of Iowa will monitor air quality.
Environmentalist Jassim al-Asadi stands on a boat and looks out over the marshes where he grew up in southern Iraq. Despite having been kidnapped, tortured and accused by an Iran-backed militia of being an Israeli agent, Asadi is back in the marshes.
Iraqi environmentalist Jassim al-Asadi has dedicated his life to protecting Iraq's ancient marshlands. He even helped reflood areas that Saddam Hussein drained and set fire to decades ago to flush out resistance fighters. In February 2023, an Iran-backed militia kidnapped and tortured Asadi for two weeks on false charges that he was an Israeli spy who had ignited anti-government protests. He endured the trauma by reciting poetry until his Bani Asad tribe mobilized armed tribal fighters to secure his release. Once freed, he refused European asylum so he could continue his work. Today, despite drought and other hardships on the land, Asadi continues to monitor recovering water levels as wildlife slowly starts to return to the marshes.

items.title: Ukraine war briefing: Trump ‘open’ to Kyiv getting Nato-like mutual defence guarantee, says Kushner - The Guardian
items.summary: Ukraine war briefing: Trump ‘open’ to Kyiv getting Nato-like mutual defence guarantee, says Kushner  <font color="#6f6f6f"
items.content:
A police officer speaks with the owners of a damaged apartment at the site of a residential building hit by a Russian drone strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Thursday. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters
A police officer speaks with the owners of a damaged apartment at the site of a residential building hit by a Russian drone strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Thursday. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters
Ukraine war briefing: Trump ‘open’ to Kyiv getting Nato-like mutual defence guarantee, says Kushner
US envoy also says he believes Moscow is ‘comfortable’ with a guarantee; Russia attacks Kyiv bridges after Putin vows response for Crimea bridge attack. What we know on day 1,731
US envoy Jared Kushner has said Donald Trump is open to extending Ukraine a security guarantee similar to Nato’s mutual defence clause , but stressed that Washington has to protect its interests too. French president Emmanuel Macron meanwhile urged Kyiv’s allies to “reopen the question” of Ukraine becoming a member of the military alliance. Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, told a press conference in Germany: “From America’s perspective, giving an Article 5-like security guarantee is a really, really big deal. And I think that that’s something that President Trump is open to, but obviously it has to be in America’s interest to do that. We also have to make sure that it’s part of a broader security package.”
Kushner’s comments came after Ukraine’s allies gathered for a summit of the “coalition of the willing” in Berlin with Volodymyr Zelenskyy to emphasise support for Kyiv nearly five years since Russia’s 2022 invasion, and to push for a European role in future peace negotiations. Kushner added on Thursday that “we’ve gotten the Russians comfortable with that concept, where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5 ”. He noted that went with Moscow’s intention to “not have another war” when this conflict was over, while acknowledging “scepticism” over the position.
Macron called on Ukraine’s allies to do the “maximum” to deliver the air defence systems it needed, as well as looking again at Ukraine joining Nato . “Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine’s accession to Nato,” the French president said in Berlin. “Everyone who has the capacity to provide the means to defend and protect Ukrainian citizens must do so now,” he said, adding the priority was to deploy anti-missile systems and interceptors.
Vladimir Putin said Russia’s response to the bombing of the Kerch bridge to Crimea would be “painful” , after Ukraine attacked the strategic connection for the third time this week. The Russian president claimed he had considered agreeing to local ceasefires until the Kerch road bridge was destroyed, report Dan Sabbagh and Jakub Krupa .
On Friday, after Putin’s threat, a Russian ballistic missile attack hit three ⁠bridges on Kyiv’s Dnipro River and killed three people , the city’s mayor said, in the ⁠biggest strikes on routes ⁠connecting ​the left and right banks of Ukraine’s capital since the war began. The missiles hit the ⁠ Podilsko-Voskresenskyi bridge crossing as well as the Darnytskyi and Pivdennyi bridges , Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram, resulting in closure or ⁠traffic restrictions. About ‌15 people were injured, he added. The strikes also caused fires ‌and damaged critical infrastructure and buildings. In the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, a Russian drone damaged a hospital, wounding four people, mayor Igor Terekhov said. In ‌Russian-controlled Luhansk, three ⁠people ​were ⁠killed ⁠in ​a Ukrainian ‌attack, said Russian-installed ‌authorities of ​the ⁠eastern Ukrainian ​region.
The summit of the coalition of the willing on Thursday was co-hosted by the leaders of Germany, Britain and France shortly after unprecedented three-way talks in China between Trump, Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping. China, Russia and the US said after their talks they had agreed to a peace statement, but the declaration made no mention of the war in Ukraine. The European coalition’s meeting in Berlin expressed indignation at the trilateral’s cosy optics, reports Rebecca Bailey . “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump.
German chancellor Friedrich Merz said he expected new Ukraine peace talks would “take place soon” , with Europe now set to have a seat at the table alongside the US, Russia and Ukraine. Merz, speaking in Berlin, did not give a date and added that “we are looking for locations on neutral ground”, naming the United Arab Emirates as a possible location. British prime minister Andy Burnham said: “I hope that message is heard very clearly in Moscow. For as long as it takes, we will be there at the side of Ukraine and we will not falter.”
A wave of daytime Russian strikes on Kyiv on Thursday killed one person and damaged the historic Saint Volodymyr Cathedral as well as the embassies of Austria and the Netherlands. “Russia has been terrorising Kyiv with drones all day ... At least four people are known to be injured so far, and one person was killed,” prime minister Sergiy Koretsky said.

By Lily Jamali North America Technology correspondent
California has served an investigative subpoena on the AI chip designer Nvidia in the wake of a scandal that ended in the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang.
The state's top law enforcement officer, attorney general Rob Bonta, said he is probing whether Nvidia or Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, adding that such actions could violate California law if the company is found to have mislead investors and the public.
"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said on Thursday.

Nvidia has its global headquarters in Santa Clara, California.
Earlier this month, it emerged that Huang had an extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was an executive at the Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.
Some members of the US Congress have urged the Department of Commerce to investigate whether Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer, diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Megaspeed has previously said it is aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
Nvidia shares have plummeted 22% since the New York Times reported on the affair in early November.
Earlier this week, the company's board chair Harvey Jones said Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Jensen Huang after the longtime Nvidia boss and co-founder issued a statement saying he would be "honoured" to return, as some tech leaders including Elon Musk campaigned on his behalf.

UK operation wards off risk of cyber-attack on supermarket fridges and freezers
News of vulnerability comes after retailers in at least seven European countries hit by cyber-attacks
A secret government cybersecurity operation recently warded off the risk of a cyber-attack on fridges and freezers in UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums, it has emerged.
An attack would have been similar to those that have caused many millions of euros of damage in continental Europe in recent months. But, while many retailers have now been protected, researchers warned that many more could still be vulnerable.
News of the operation led by Whitehall and the National Cyber Security Centre, first reported by the BBC, follows a cyberattack this month of supermarket chains in at least seven European countries.
Another wave of attacks also affected hundreds of retailers across France in October in an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression” for which Paris has publicly blamed Iran . The Pentagon is also investigating a suspected hack after a series of fridge malfunctions hit at least six US military bases in August.
The French fridge hacks were relatively unsophisticated. An AI-enabled attack would raise the stakes
Experts told the Guardian that if the vulnerability in UK-based devices had been discovered and exploited before a fix was found, the consequences would have been serious.
“This incident should serve as a wake-up call for the entire refrigeration industry,” said Garry Turner-Smith of Omega Solutions, a refrigeration consultancy firm whose employee, Neil McCourt, found the vulnerability in devices manufactured by Resource Data Management (RDM).
He said: “Had these weaknesses been discovered and exploited by someone with malicious intentions, they could have gained full control of vulnerable RDM data managers and used that access to interfere with refrigeration systems across multiple sites. This raises the prospect of attacks similar to those seen in Europe.”
After Omega was alerted to the weakness, the firm called in the cybersecurity consultants Pen Test Partners to investigate. Both firms then raised their concerns with the manufacturer, RDM.
Ken Munro, Pen Test Partners’ managing partner, said: “We determined that there was an urgent requirement to alert supermarkets and the food supply chain to the issue and fix. “However, we also had to work quietly to avoid alerting less ethical hackers and nation states of the likes of Iran, who are active in this space.”
Munro was attending a retail industry cyber event the day the vulnerabilities were found, enabling him to meet National Cyber Security Centre representatives in person to share the intelligence.
That triggered a series of briefing calls between retailers and officials from the National Cyber Security Centre, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs and the Food Standards Agency, among others, Munro said.
Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?
He added that Pen Test Partners had also tried to alert the owners of exposed devices. “Some controllers were easy to identify and thus contact the owners, but many thousands at small stores are still exposed,” he said.
“The vulnerability is not easy to find for a number of reasons, but once the method is known, it’s easy to recreate. We have not published that method, so there is still time for small operators to take their controllers off the public internet and/or apply the updated firmware.”
A National Cyber Security Centre spokesperson said it had “shared important insight and security advice to ensure that organisations understood potential risks to their networks, and were taking the appropriate measures to mitigate them”.
RDM did not respond to a request for comment. Its chief executive, Ged Evans, told the BBC the vulnerability was “identified in a test environment” that “went beyond” what such exercises usually involved as it “included dismantling our hardware”.
Evans saidd: “In any event we have acted at pace to address this issue and have already deployed first patch releases and have been in proactive contact with our customers to flag any issues and recommend mitigatory steps.”

Norway’s Gas Sales Surge Nearly 20% as Europe Braces for Winter
By Jan-Thore Bergsagel - Nov 20, 2026, 10:30 AM CST
Norway's daily gas sales jumped nearly 20% in October and were 5.6% above year-earlier levels. The rebound comes as the EU heads into winter with its gas storage facilities less than 70% full.
Norway sold 11 billion cubic meters of natural gas in October, up 2.1 billion cubic meters from September, according to preliminary figures from the Norwegian Offshore Directorate. Daily sales averaged 355.6 million cubic meters, up from a revised 296.8 million in September and 2.2% above the regulator's forecast.
EU gas storage was 69.8% full on November 18, down from a late-October peak of about 75%, according to Gas Infrastructure Europe data. The EU held about 791 terawatt-hours of gas in storage, roughly 12% less than a year earlier. That leaves buyers with a smaller buffer as heating demand rises.
Norwegian gas sales also rose sharply between September and October last year. This October, Norway sold nearly 19 million cubic meters more per day than it did a year earlier. Nearly all Norwegian gas is exported, with most of it reaching European markets by pipeline.
Norwegian crude production also recovered from September, rising by 146,000 barrels per day to 1.843 million bpd. Output beat the regulator's forecast by 103,000 bpd but remained 3.1% below October 2025. Total liquids production, including natural gas liquids and condensate, climbed to 2.03 million bpd, down 3.4% from a year earlier.
Across oil, gas and other liquids, Norway produced about 1.27 billion barrels of oil equivalent in the first ten months of 2026, roughly 32 million boe, or 2.5%, more than in the same period last year. Gas accounted for just over half of that volume at about 649 million boe. Crude contributed around 564 million barrels, and natural gas liquids and condensate added another 60 million barrels. Crude output through October was 4.1% above the offshore regulator's forecast. In October alone, higher gas sales more than offset the year-on-year decline in liquids output, lifting combined petroleum production by 1% on an oil-equivalent basis.

Hormuz Oil Exports Could Decline amid Inbound Tanker Shortage
The increased flows of oil from the Strait of Hormuz, mostly thanks to ship-to-ship (STS) transfers in the Gulf of Oman, are tying up supertankers for weeks waiting for the transfers outside the Strait
The market and most analysts assume that the steady flow of crude oil from the Strait of Hormuz and the entire Middle Eastern region will continue into the next months.
Analysts are touting the remarkable recovery in crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf, which have jumped close to pre-war levels in recent months.
The oil market reflects the bearish sentiment, with Brent Crude prices sliding in the past weeks to around $92 per barrel, down from a recent peak of over $118 per barrel in late October.
The market and most analysts assume that the steady flow of crude oil from the Strait of Hormuz and the entire Middle Eastern region will continue into the next months, rebalancing supply and demand and even tipping the balance into a large surplus next year.
However, in the volatile situation in and around the Strait of Hormuz, with no recent rapprochement for potential U.S.-Iran talks, nothing is given, and no forecast has more than 50/50 odds of panning out.
The Iran war has reshuffled trade routes and patterns and tied up more tankers in inefficient and lengthy voyages.
The increased flows of oil from the Strait of Hormuz, mostly thanks to ship-to-ship (STS) transfers in the Gulf of Oman, are tying up supertankers for weeks waiting for the transfers outside the Strait, limiting the availability of very large crude carriers (VLCCs) for the other global key oil trade routes, such as the U.S. Gulf Coast to Asia.
The inefficient shuttle shipping is tying up a growing number of smaller vessels, Suezmaxes and Aframaxes, too, on the Hormuz trade.
This leaves fewer available empty tankers globally willing to travel to the Middle East to pick up cargoes in the Gulf of Oman.
The total capacity of the empty tankers going to the Middle East has slumped by some 40% since the end of August, per data from Tankertrackers.com cited by Bloomberg .
There are “not enough vacant tankers to take oil out of the region,” Tankertrackers.com’s co-founder, Samir Madani, told the publication.
“It’s one thing to bring the oil out into the Gulf of Oman via the Strait of Hormuz, but it seems like there isn’t enough to take the oil out of the Gulf of Oman,” the analyst said.
As of November 16, the combined capacity of ballasting supertankers and Suezmaxes en route to the Gulf of Oman has slumped to 71 million barrels, down from 130 million barrels capacity at the end of August, according to data compiled by Tankertrackers.com.
To be sure, flows from the Middle East remain elevated, albeit somewhat lower so far in November compared to October. Crude oil exports from the Strait of Hormuz have held so far despite the worst month for attacks on tankers in the area since the war began.
The high crude oil export levels despite increased security risks give the market and many analysts confidence that the only path forward is continuous recovery and, ultimately, an oil glut within months.
Tanker rates have dropped from the record highs seen in early October, but they remain above historical norms and pre-war levels amid heightened war insurance premiums and security risks.
“Security risks continue to weigh on tanker operations in the Gulf,” Maria Bertzeletou, Senior Market Analyst at Signal Group, wrote in an analysis this week.
“Repeated attacks continue to restrict the pool of owners willing to accept Gulf employment, while elevated war-risk insurance costs and operational delays add to voyage expenses and limit effective vessel availability.”
So far this month, Iran has been reporting nearly daily incidents of tankers hitting naval mines in corridors that Iran has designated as “unauthorized” in the Strait of Hormuz.
Non-Iranian observers and organizations also report more frequent attacks on tankers in and near the Strait of Hormuz.
Five tankers have been struck near Hormuz in the week between November 11 and 18, according to remote-sensing intelligence by Windward .
“This highlights Iran’s continued strategy of maritime attrition, and it is unlikely to ease unless diplomatic conditions change,” the maritime intelligence firm said on Wednesday.
Despite the threat to tanker shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, investment banks and the International Energy Agency (IEA) expect the crude oil market to be in a surplus as early as this quarter.
“We continue to expect the oil balance to loosen as supply recovers, limiting the scope for a sustained rebound in prices,” ING’s commodities strategists Ewa Manthey and Warren Patterson said in a Wednesday note.
In its November monthly report , the IEA said that the global oil market will return to a surplus this quarter, with a more substantial build in 2027.
“As always, downside risks to the forecast persist, as attacks on shipping undermine maritime security, which is pivotal to a sustained recovery,” the agency noted.
Goldman Sachs Research’s latest forecast calls for oil prices easing gradually in 2027 as suppliers in the Middle East adapt to disruption from the war in Iran.
Goldman’s commodities analysts expect Brent Crude to average $88 per barrel in 2027 under their base case assumption of no definitive diplomatic breakthrough in Iran and no re-escalation with major long-term damage to oil infrastructure.
Under the same base case scenario, Goldman Sachs forecasts that Brent will fall from around $92 per barrel today to $78 by early December 2027 “as a sizable surplus decreases Brent’s fair value from $90 per barrel today to the high $70s by the end of 2027.”

Hormuz, LNG & Electrification: The IEA World Energy Outlook
Fatih Birol, Executive Director of the IEA. Credit for headshot: WEF
The IEA’s World Energy Outlook 2026 calls the Hormuz disruption the largest supply shock on record, as electrification and energy security reshape markets
The International Energy Agency (IEA) has published its World Energy Outlook 2026, and it opens with a sobering verdict.
The disruption to the flow of oil and gas through the Strait of Hormuz this year is the largest energy supply shock the world has faced, the agency says, and as of November it is far from over.
The Strait is the narrow waterway at the mouth of the Gulf through which a large share (around one-fifth) of the world’s oil and LNG ordinarily passes.
Cumulative losses from the Gulf now stand at 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres of gas.
The system has absorbed much of that, but the IEA says the burden is increasingly falling on consumers as other buffers run down.
Diesel, which the report calls the workhorse of the global economy, has hit record prices above US$200 a barrel, which has left many motorists, farmers and business owners reeling.
Before the crisis, around 80% of the oil and almost 90% of the LNG passing through the Strait was bound for Asia.
That helps explain why developing economies in Asia-Pacific and Africa are among the worst affected, and why more than four billion people live in countries that rely on the Strait for over 30% of their oil.
"The Hormuz crisis has delivered a huge shock to the energy system, dwarfing the scale of past crises," said Fatih Birol, the Executive Director of the IEA this week.
"The longer it lasts, the deeper the effects. Diversification, domestically available resources and electrification are set to be the big winners."
Cumulative loss in oil supply during selected crises from 1956-2026, measured in billions of barrels. Credit: IEA
Rather than a single forecast, the report offers several scenarios that differ in how governments respond.
The Current Policies Scenario (CPS) assumes only measures already firmly in place.
The Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS) adds proposals that have been formally put forward but not yet adopted.
Both assume that transit through the Strait is unimpeded by the end of 2027.
The Additional Response Case (ARC) asks what happens if the crisis drags on and governments implement measures that are currently only under consideration.
The Low Hormuz Case (LHC) goes further and asks whether the world could manage without the Strait at all.
In the STEPS, oil demand levels off at around 103 million barrels per day (mb/d) by 2030 before a slow decline.
In the ARC, oil use is more than 4 mb/d lower than that by 2035.
Around 7 mb/d of new pipelines that would let Gulf producers avoid the Strait are under construction or consideration.
Building them would cost an estimated US$40bn and add around US$2 to the cost of each barrel exported.
Even if every project is completed, the LHC only reduces the need for transit to 2 mb/d by 2035.
The IEA adds that alternative routes are likely to be vulnerable too if the Middle East is unstable.
Gas presents a different risk, with a wave of new export projects led by the United States set to expand LNG supply by more than 50% if all of them proceed.
If wary Asian importers invest less in terminals and pipelines because of the crisis, the report warns of a lasting imbalance once Middle East supply returns at scale.
The IEA released its emergency reserve of fuel earlier this year in an attempt to soften the blow of the Strait of Hormuz crisis. Credit: IEA
Electricity accounts for around 23% of final energy consumption, and demand has grown by 3.3% a year since 2019, against 2.9% for the global economy.
Solar PV added 600 terawatt-hours of generation in 2025, the third-largest single-year increase ever achieved by any source.
Renewables supply 33% of electricity today and reach 45-50% by 2035 in both the CPS and STEPS.
Nuclear is also returning, with nearly 90GW under construction, the highest level in more than 35 years.
Meanwhile, at least 25 million kilometres of new power lines will be needed over the next decade, and surging data centre demand is already straining some markets.
Fatih Birol gave a press conference this week to discuss the findings of the IEA's report. Credit: IEA
The report is blunt that energy security alone will not deliver adequate climate action.
The ARC brings warming in 2100 to 2.4°C against 2.5°C in the STEPS, partly because higher coal use offsets gains elsewhere. The CPS points to around 2.9°C.
The human cost is stark too, with around 720 million people still without electricity and nearly two billion relying on polluting cooking methods.
Spending on imported oil and gas is set to reach US$1.6tn in 2026, 25% higher than in 2025, even though demand is down.
A resolution could bring cheaper fuel, but the IEA reminds readers that energy markets move in cycles and high prices are likely to return.
Fatih Birol, who has been in Türkiye this week for COP31, tied the report's findings to the consensus that the world's nations are attempting to establish at the summit.
"Today’s energy crisis is moving the world deeper into the Age of Electricity with many countries looking to reduce reliance on fuel imports," he said.
"By 2035, electricity is set to be closing in on 30% of final energy use, up from 23% now. The 35x35 Pledge at COP31 can accelerate progress further."

items.content:
With Oil Revenue Running Out, Iran Teases Breaking US Blockade
With Oil Revenue Running Out, Iran Teases Breaking US Blockade
Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, on October 2
With Iran's revenue from crude oil and condensate exports projected to hit zero by mid-December, hardline commentators and outlets close to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) are increasingly advocating a direct challenge to the US naval blockade of Iranian ports and waters.
Their proposal is for a declared "convoy of tankers" to sail through the blockade, accompanied by threats to target the oil infrastructure of Iran's Gulf neighbors if US forces attack Iranian vessels.
Iranian forces already attempted attacks on US targets in Bahrain and Kuwait this week.
A campaign promoting the idea of breaking the blockade gathered pace on November 19, when the IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency published a column making the case for a “convoy of oil tankers.”
The same day, the ship-tracking service TankerTrackers.com said in a one-line post on X that “Iran appears to be preparing to ship out oil again.”
No Iranian official body has formally announced such a plan, but the discussion shows how hard the US blockade is biting.
Even Hard-Liners Balk As Iran 'Quietly' Caps Subsidized Bread
The closest thing to an official signal came from IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi. On November 19, he told a gathering in Tehran, “We will not allow the continued naval, land, and air blockade imposed on our country.”
To make its case, the Fars column reached back to the Shahnameh, Iran's national epic. When the mythical hero Fereydun reaches the Arvand River on his way to overthrow the tyrant Zahhak, the guardian of the river refuses him boats. Fereydun does not wait. He and his men ride their horses into the water and cross.
“We will not wait for America's permission,” Fars argued. “We open the route and raise the cost of closing it so high that the other side's reason tells it to leave it open.”
Fars warned that any attack on an Iranian tanker could prompt Tehran to retaliate against oil facilities across the Persian Gulf, specifically naming those in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates.
The proposal quickly gained traction among hardline figures, some of whom appeared to present it as an impending decision rather than a suggestion.
Tit-For-Tat US-Iran Attacks Persist As Peace Deal Remains Elusive
Lawmaker Ebrahim Azizi, chairman of the parliament’s influential national security and foreign policy committee, declared in English on X that Iran “cannot be blockaded” and ended his post with an hourglass emoji.
Hard-line pundit Ruhollah Jomei wrote of “the Islamic republic's decision to load crude oil and dispatch a tanker to China” -- the biggest buyer of Iranian oil.
Mojtaba Najafi, whom some Iranian media claim is close to circles of power, wrote, “Apparently, Tehran no longer wants to be a spectator to the blockade and threats.”
If the reports are true, Iran is looking to “actively challenge the blockade,” said Hamidreza Azizi, an analyst with the International Crisis Group.
Writing on X, he argued that if a tanker gets through, the blockade loses credibility. If US forces stop or strike it, Tehran gains a direct trigger for retaliation. Azizi added that Iran was seeking "to take the military initiative while leaving Washington with the responsibility for triggering the next escalation."
According to the energy-intelligence firm Kpler, Iran's revenue from crude oil and condensate exports could fall to zero by mid-December, for the first time in the country's history.
The effects of the blockade are already visible in the country's oil shipments. Kpler's data shows that the volume of Iranian oil on the water outside the blockade zone peaked at 88.8 million barrels on July 14, when the blockade was reimposed. By mid-October, that figure had fallen to zero as the last cargoes were discharged in China.
Another 43 million barrels remain stranded inside the blockade area, leaving Tehran with a dwindling stockpile of oil that can be delivered to buyers.
Speaking to RFE/RL's Radio Farda, Kpler senior commodity analyst Homayoun Falakshahi cautioned against interpreting recent developments as evidence that Iran was preparing a concerted effort to break the blockade.
"In our view, it is still too early to say that Iran has taken serious action to break the naval blockade," he said.
Kpler has identified about 20 tankers near Kharg Island, Iran's main oil export terminal, Falakshahi said. Most have already loaded their cargoes but remain stationary, apparently waiting for the blockade to be lifted before attempting to move. Kpler has observed only one tanker moving so far.
There has, however, been at least one notable development. On November 17, Kpler detected an Iranian tanker carrying crude transferring its cargo to another vessel. The receiving tanker was one typically used to transport Russian fuel oil, Falakshahi said.
But he cautioned against reading too much into the transfer, saying it could have been prompted by a technical problem aboard the first vessel rather than forming part of a broader effort to circumvent the blockade.
Iran typically conducts ship-to-ship transfers near Malaysia or off the coast of Oman, rather than close to Kharg Island, he added.
"I think we have to wait for the next few days and see whether more tankers try to move," Falakshahi said.
The United States first blockaded Iranian ports on April 13, after US-Iran talks in Islamabad collapsed. It lifted the blockade on June 18 under a memorandum of understanding signed the previous day.
As that deal unraveled, Washington reimposed the blockade on July 14, and it has remained in place since. In total, Iranian ports have been under blockade for about 195 days, including the last 129 without a break.
With Soaring Prices And Police Crackdowns, Free Time Now Costs Too Much For Tehran's Youth
The blockade is imposing high costs on Washington as well, both financially and in terms of military resources.
At a Senate hearing this week, Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren cited independent estimates that it costs about $32.5 million a day, a figure acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao confirmed.
Bloomberg, which produced the figure cited by Warren, has also reported that the operation ties up more than 30 percent of the US Navy's warships. The Pentagon put the overall cost of the Iran war at $48.3 billion as of November 13, not counting damage to US bases in the region.
That figure is still a fraction of the revenue Iran stands to lose. Kpler previously estimated the blockade was costing Tehran between $200 million and $250 million in lost oil revenue every day.
Elaheh Ravanshad of RFE/RL's Radio Farda contributed to this report.
With Oil Revenue Running Out, Iran Teases Breaking US Blockade
Kian Sharifi is a feature writer specializing in Iranian affairs in RFE/RL's Central Newsroom in Prague. He got his start in journalism at the Financial Tribune, an English-language newspaper published in Tehran, where he worked as an editor. He then moved to BBC Monitoring, where he led a team of journalists who closely watched media trends and analyzed key developments in Iran and the wider region.

China’s Oil Imports from Persian Gulf Jump to Wartime High
China's crude oil imports from the Persian Gulf surged by 42.4% in October from September, to the highest level since the Iran war began, as supply via the Strait of Hormuz rebounded and Gulf producers slashed prices for their crude to attract buyers amid record-high freight rates.
China imported 19.7 million tons of crude oil from the Persian Gulf producers, excluding Iran, in October, a 42.4% jump from the previous month, per calculations by the South China Morning Post based on Chinese customs data released on Friday.
October was the fourth consecutive month in which Chinese crude oil imports from the Gulf countries increased from the previous month, according to the data.
Gulf producers shipped almost half of total Chinese term supplies last month, at a level approaching the pre-war volumes, the estimates by the South China Morning Post showed.
The surge in Chinese imports from the Gulf coincided with the recovery of crude oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
Additionally, Gulf producers reduced the prices of their crude grades loading for Asia as Hormuz flows rebounded and pressured down Middle Eastern crude benchmarks.
Rising supply from the Middle East has weakened both the Dubai and Murban prices. At the end October, the prices of physical Middle East crude slumped as flows from the region recovered and reached pre-war levels on some days.
Lower prices for December are expected to continue attracting buying interest in China, especially amid the slide in international crude oil prices.
Saudi oil giant Aramco earlier this month slashed the price for its flagship Arab Light crude for Asia for loading in December by $2 per barrel, to a discount of $6.50 per barrel to the Oman/Dubai average. This is the steepest discount for Saudi crude to the Middle East's benchmark since May 2020 during the COVID pandemic.

Gold heads for worst week in eight months on dollar strength
Gold prices slipped on Friday and were headed for their worst week in eight months, as a resilient US dollar and expectations of a Federal Reserve interest-rate hike in December weighed on bullion.
Gold extended its ​sharp selloff on Friday, hovering near a more than one-year low and heading for its steepest weekly decline in eight months, as expectations of a hawkish Federal Reserve boosted ⁠the ‌dollar and Treasury yields.
Spot gold fell 1.3% to $3,576.09 per ⁠ounce, after touching its lowest level since September 4, 2025 at $3,513.54 earlier in the session. Bullion has shed about 8% this week, the most since the week ending March ‌20.
US gold futures for December delivery slid 2.9% to $3,577.60.
"Gold is under renewed pressure from hawkish Fed expectations, which are lifting real yields ​and the US dollar and raising the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset. The ongoing AI-related equity sell-off is also prompting some forced liquidations of gold positions to cover losses elsewhere," Critical MetalsCEO Tony Sage said.
The ⁠selloff gathered pace after Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulsonjoined other policymakers in flagging inflation risks that ‌could warrant another interest-rate increase, reinforcing expectations that US borrowing ‌costs will rise further.
Markets see a 99.3% chance of a 25-basis-point US rate hike in December, according to CME's FedWatch tool.
Asian sharestumbled on Friday and were headed for their worst ⁠week since 2020 after Anthropic's debut failed to restore investor confidence in the ⁠AI sector, while the dollar extended its rally on safe-haven demand.
Meanwhile, ⁠physical golddemand in India and China strengthened this week as the price slump attracted bargain hunters, with investors in China viewing the ​correction as a buying opportunity.

Wall Street's sell-off intensified on Thursday, November 19, as selling pressure spread across nearly every sector of the market. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI) plunged more than 1,100 points, falling 2.19% to 49,097 and moving closer to correction territory. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) fell 2.00% to 7,177, marking its sixth consecutive session of losses, while the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) dropped 2.23% to 23,886 as investors continued to retreat from growth stocks.
Selling pressure extended beyond equities, with gold falling 2.10% to $3,663.50. The 10-year Treasury yield eased three basis points to 5.07%, offering little relief to equity markets. Energy and consumer staples were among the few sectors to finish in positive territory, gaining 0.14% and 0.04%, respectively, while industrials plunged 2.61%.
Despite the broader market sell-off, Insmed (NASDAQ:INSM) surged 20.58% following reports that French pharmaceutical giant Sanofi (NASDAQ:SNY) is considering an acquisition of the biotechnology company. Palo Alto Networks (NASDAQ:PANW) also bucked the broader trend, gaining 6.42% after reporting stronger-than-expected quarterly earnings and announcing a $4.5 billion acquisition.
Conversely, Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) plunged 7.72% following a media report alleging ties to a blacklisted Chinese server manufacturer. The report adds another layer of regulatory uncertainty to a semiconductor industry already grappling with tightening U.S. export restrictions and deteriorating investor sentiment.
Perhaps the most concerning development on Wall Street is how broadly selling pressure has spread. What initially appeared to be a pullback driven by elevated technology valuations is increasingly developing into a broader market downturn. Even Nvidia 's (NASDAQ:NVDA) exceptional quarterly earnings have failed to reverse sentiment, suggesting that concerns surrounding inflation, interest rates, and stock valuations are taking precedence over strong corporate results.
Looking ahead, investors should pay particularly close attention to Treasury yields and the U.S. dollar. With the Federal Reserve signaling that further interest rate hikes may be necessary, persistently restrictive financial conditions could put additional pressure on corporate earnings and stock valuations heading into 2027.
Walmart's (NASDAQ:WMT) upcoming quarterly earnings report will also provide an important assessment of consumer spending heading into the holiday shopping season. While recent results from Target (NYSE:TGT) and TJX Companies, Inc. (NYSE:TJX) have been encouraging, any signs of weakening consumer demand could introduce another headwind for equities.

California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state
Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded
Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.
Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.
A large wave pours over the seawall in Pacifica. Photograph: Fred Greaves/Reuters Nearly 72,000 people have been evacuated from areas of Odisha in eastern India as Tropical Cyclone Akvan approaches land. Akvan is expected to make landfall on Friday between Narsapur and Puri, prompting cyclone warnings from the India Meteorological Department for north Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and south Odisha coasts. Peak wind gusts are expected to reach 70mph, with rainfall totals through Friday and Saturday potentially exceeding 200mm for northern coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.
Fishers carry a boat to a safer place along the shore before the expected landfall of Tropical Cyclone Akvan near Gopalpur in Odisha, India. Photograph: Reuters After a yellow level 2 severe thunderstorm warning by the South African Weather Service on Tuesday, torrential rainfall and large hail were reported across parts of Johannesburg. The storms triggered flash flooding and caused infrastructure damage in the township of Soweto. One person died, while another remains missing after the severe storms.

items.title: More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
items.summary: African countries at the UN climate summit in Turkey are demanding more funding from developed nations to help them cope with climate change.
items.content:
Image caption, Africa is pushing for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035, from an annual $40bn (Â£30bn)
By Navin Singh Khadka Environmental correspondent, BBC World Service
In Uganda's northern Karamoja region, Elijah Lobur and his family now eat just one meal a day.
A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops, while food brought in from elsewhere has become increasingly unaffordable.
"Seven months without rain has brought us to this point where we now live in hunger," the 44-year-old farmer, who lives with his grandmother, wife and five children, told the BBC.
"Even some of the wild plants that we used to eat have withered and dried up."
Local officials say more than 90% of crops have failed in the region, where agriculture is largely rain-fed.
Further south, in Malawi, Mathews Nkhambala has experienced the devastating effects of flooding.
In April 2024, barely a year after Tropical Cyclone Freddy devastated the country's southern region, floods displaced people in Chikwawa district.
Nkhambala fled to higher ground with his wife and four children as floodwaters swept through his village.
"As we reached a safe height, we saw our house swept away right in front of our eyes. Everything I had was gone," he told the BBC.
He lost a harvest of 15 bags of sorghum and part of his farmland. His children were so traumatised that they stopped going to school.
"They refused to go to school for many months. They were so disturbed," he recalled.
After relocating and trying to rebuild his life, Nkhambala is now facing another climate challenge - this time a lack of rain.
"This time we fear there may be no harvest. I have no clue what I will do."
A government assessment after Cyclone Freddy found that Malawi had experienced more than 50 disasters linked to storms, floods, landslides and droughts since 1980, affecting millions of people.
While Uganda and Malawi are suffering the effects of climate change and their governments are asking for assistance adapting to the new global weather patterns, they are among 23 African countries yet to submit National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) to the UN climate convention secretariat.
These are the plans that detail how climate change has affected them and the risks they face, and so help make a case for what assistance they need. Without them, experts say, it becomes difficult to secure funding.
"Our region has experienced cyclical droughts for decades, but there has been no action plan to tackle these climate impacts," said Milton Lorpia, who works for Warrior Squad Foundation in Karamoja region of Uganda.
"If only such a plan were in place and implemented, it would certainly have helped us."
Image caption, Mathews Nkhambala and his wife fear their harvest may fail this year
The African Group of Negotiators at the ongoing UN climate summit (COP31) in Turkey is pushing for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035, from an annual $40bn (Â£30bn) baseline that it says developed countries committed to providing by 2025. The interpretation of that commitment remains contested.
The proposal was not accepted for formal negotiations at the summit, although African negotiators have continued to push for it.
The funding is intended to help vulnerable countries prepare for and withstand climate change-induced extreme weather, such as droughts, floods and wildfires.
But the European Union, one of the largest providers of climate finance, says the priority should be ensuring existing commitments reach vulnerable countries rather than setting new funding targets.
"We haven't come to the table with additional monies or additional capital. It's about what we have committed already and ensuring it's deployed," Darragh O'Brien, who leads the EU delegation at COP31 on behalf of the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, told a press conference.
He acknowledged that developing countries faced difficulties accessing available funding, saying the process needed to be improved.
Wopke Hoekstra, the European Commission's climate commissioner, also argued that the summit should focus on delivering existing pledges rather than making new ones.
"If you are a vulnerable nation in the Pacific or one of the LDCs (Least Developed Countries) and the money is in the bank but does not land on the ground then it is effectively meaningless," he said.
'It can kill us': Kenyans fear impact of El NiÃ±o with floods predicted
Hoekstra said the EU had provided $30bn of the $100bn in climate finance committed by developed countries in recent years, adding that other wealthy nations should contribute more.
The scale of the need is substantial. According to the UN's Adaptation Gap Report published last year, sub-Saharan Africa requires about $51bn annually in adaptation finance, while the Middle East and North Africa needs $112bn.
Globally, developing countries will need about $300bn annually by 2035, according to the UN's latest report. Yet they received only about 10% of that amount from developed countries in 2024.
Climate-related loss and damage in Africa is projected to cost $440bn between 2020 and 2030, according to Nairobi-based think tank Power Shift Africa.
Under the 2015 Paris climate agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations, including for climate adaptation.
But why have so many African countries failed to prepare plans that could help them identify their needs and build resilience?
"If you look closely, the countries that are yet to submit their NAPs are already dealing with multiple crises, including debt distress, economic pressures and other issues," said David Abudho, climate justice lead at the aid agency, Oxfam.
"Their governments' ability to invest in climate adaptation is limited."
Sheila Apiny, regional climate justice adviser at ActionAid, said the lack of plans reflected a wider shortage of financial and technical support.
"The absence of NAPs in so many countries is, in itself, evidence of an adaptation finance and capacity gap," she argued.
She said this created a vicious cycle - countries lack support to prepare their plans, while not having the plans makes it harder to secure funding for climate resilience.
"When countries lack adequate adaptation planning and, more importantly, the resources to implement those plans, governments are forced into a cycle of responding to disasters instead of preventing or reducing their impacts," said Amos Wemanya, senior climate adviser at Power Shift Africa.
"Instead of investing in early warning systems, climate-resilient agriculture, water security and flood protection, scarce public resources are repeatedly diverted towards emergency relief and reconstruction. This costs more over time and leaves communities increasingly vulnerable."
Image caption, Under the 2015 Paris climate agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations, including for climate adaptation
African negotiators acknowledge that adaptation plans help countries prioritise investments and attract funding, but argue that their absence should not be used to deny them financial support.
"Of course, having a comprehensive NAP helps countries prioritise investments and prepare proposals for climate finance," said Mahlet Eyassu Melkie, a senior strategic adviser to Ethiopia's COP32 presidency.
"But Africa's adaptation financing needs are based on scientific assessments, climate vulnerability, national priorities and regional estimates â not simply on whether every country has submitted a particular planning document."
The UN Development Programme, which has helped more than 45 countries prepare their plans, said NAPs can help governments mobilise international support and coordinate climate action.
Fred Njehu, a Pan-African political strategist at Greenpeace Africa, said their absence could nevertheless create significant obstacles.
"It is fair to acknowledge that missing adaptation plans act as a major functional barrier that severely bottlenecks the speed, volume and quality of international funding a country can access," he said.
But having a plan does not guarantee the money needed to implement it.
"Even countries that have completed their NAPs have not received money anywhere near what they require for implementation of their adaptation plans," Apiny said.
Kenya offers an example of how adaptation measures can help communities cope with climate pressures.
Image caption, The walls of the sand dams store water underground when the rivers dry up
In the country's arid and semi-arid south-east, concrete sand dams slow the flow of seasonal rivers, allowing sand to accumulate and store water underground. Communities can access it during dry periods using hand pumps or by scooping it out.
UK charity Sand Dams Worldwide and its local partner, the Africa Sand Dam Foundation, said they had built about 1,300 such dams, improving access to water as droughts become more frequent and intense.
But many vulnerable communities elsewhere on the continent are still waiting for similar interventions.
Back in drought-hit Karamoja, Lobur wonders how different things might have been if farmers had access to small-scale irrigation schemes.
"We do have some underground water sources in some places. If there were proper plans and programmes, we could have tapped them to grow food, but we are having to live in hunger instead," Lobur said.
"My grandmother keeps reminding us how she lost eight children during a famine-like situation in 1982, and we all fear we might perish like that too."

items.title: Trump, Putin, Xi pledge to increase global petrol supplies – but how?
items.summary: Analysts are sceptical about how this will be achieved amid the ongoing wars in Ukraine and Iran.
items.content:
Share Trump, Putin, Xi pledge to increase global petrol supplies – but how? on social media
The Bryan Mound Strategic Petroleum Reserve, an oil storage facility, is seen in this aerial photograph over Freeport, Texas, the United States [File: Adrees Latif/Reuters]
The United States, China and Russia have pledged to increase petrol supplies as the wars in Iran – started by Israel and the US – and Ukraine – started by Russia – continue to upend global energy markets.
Following their trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday, US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin said in a joint statement that they “plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”.

The three leaders also “reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows”.
But analysts are sceptical about how this will actually work amid the US having little to no spare refining capacity, Russia being constrained by continued Ukrainian attacks on its energy infrastructure and China’s crude oil imports disrupted by the US and Israel’s war on Iran.
“The trilateral statement should be treated as political noise rather than the first step to boosting global fuel supplies,” Hamad Hussain, a senior climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, told Al Jazeera.
“The announcement sounds like it is designed to placate consumers and constituencies. Previous efforts to increase supply [like the US-Russian diesel deal] went nowhere,” Frederic Schneider, a nonresident senior fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, told Al Jazeera.
China and the US are the world’s biggest oil refiners by capacity, followed by Russia and India.
China has roughly 18.5 to 18.83 million barrels per day (bpd) of oil refining capacity. But refining in the country is dependent on its crude oil imports, which have been badly disrupted by the continuing US-Iran conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, through which Gulf oil exporters normally ship crude oil – much of it to Asia.
According to a November report by the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), crude oil refinery imports in China fell by 2.1 million bpd in the second quarter of 2026 and by an additional 0.8 million barrels bpd in the third quarter of the year.
As of January 1 this year, the US had an operable crude oil distillation capacity of about 18.16 million bpd. Production has increased since the war began, and is already running at near full capacity.
According to an October EIA report, “the US refinery fleet has run at higher-than-normal rates this year, with refinery utilisation averaging more than 95 percent of capacity between May and September, the highest for those months since 1998”.
Russia has roughly 6.5 million bpd of oil refining capacity, according to the International Energy Agency.
But Ukrainian drone strikes on its energy infrastructure have severely impacted its refining capacity. “In June, Russian refinery throughput fell to 3.8 million barrels per day, its lowest level in more than 20 years and roughly 30 percent below a year earlier,” a September International Energy Agency report noted.
Meanwhile, India has an oil refining capacity of about 5.36 million bpd, according to government figures. But New Delhi is also heavily dependent on crude oil imports, and this has been affected by blockades in the Strait of Hormuz.
According to the EIA, US refineries are currently running at close to maximum capacity.
This has been driven largely by “tight global supplies for distillate fuel oil, leading to high international demand for US distillate fuel oil exports”, a November EIA report states. Distillate fuel oil is refined petroleum which includes diesel fuels and light fuel oils.
Hussain said that while it may be profitable to refine more oil amid higher oil prices this year, the issue is that Washington “does not have spare capacity” to do so.
The Trump administration says it is determined to boost global fuel supply and US Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said his department is “talking about reopening every refinery we can” to do so.
According to a November 19 Reuters report, US refiner Valero Energy agreed to buy the century-old LyondellBasell Industries refinery near Houston, Texas, in October and restore a portion of the facility, adding 165,000 bpd of processing capacity by the end of 2027.
The plan would reverse years of refinery closures in the US and add about 1 percent to overall US refining capacity of 18 million bpd, Reuters reported. But analysts say the total price tag of acquiring and recommissioning this refinery could reach $1bn.
Since last year, long-range Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries have resulted in serious fuel shortages across the country.
According to the IEA, in the first eight months of 2026, a Russian refinery was hit on average once every three days.
Reuters has reported that drone attacks have slashed Russian oil refineries’ combined crude processing volumes by 45 percent since late October and several regions have also begun limiting fuel.
On Friday, Reuters also reported that the Russia-installed governor of Crimea’s Sevastopol region, Mikhail Razvozhayev, said petrol sales there were being limited to one full car tank and 20 litres (5.3 gallons) in jerrycans at a number of pumping stations from Thursday.
He said the measures were being introduced to prevent people from filling canisters with hundreds of litres at a time, causing queues and preventing others from refilling.
The Siberian city of Tomsk also capped sales of petrol and diesel to 30 and 50 litres, respectively, from last week, according to local authorities.
On Thursday, the city of Penza, 770km (480 miles) southeast of Moscow, restricted petrol sales to 50 litres while limiting diesel to 200 litres per vehicle. At least half a dozen other regions introduced restrictions earlier this month.
With Ukrainian attacks continuing and Russia limiting fuel, refining more is currently a challenge for the country.
According to a November EIA report, Russia is also a major fuel exporter, especially of diesel. So any issues with its refining and decline in its exports will have a global impact.
While Trump and Putin agreed on a deal in October to allow some Russian diesel exports, none of the shipped fuel has reached customers, as traders have refused to take it .
The EIA noted that Russia’s loss of refinery operations has also “reduced refining activity in Asia and the Middle East, contributing to diesel prices increasing to the highest nominal levels on record in September”.
The conflict in the Strait of Hormuz strained crude oil imports to China earlier this year, but these have largely recovered.
While Beijing does not officially disclose the volumes of crude flowing into or out of its strategic and commercial stockpiles, Reuters reported that the world’s largest crude importer saw arrivals of 9.88 million bpd in October, up 9.4 percent from September’s 9.03 million bpd and the most since March, just after the war began.
Before the Iran war began on February 28, China was purchasing an average of 10.5 million barrels of crude per day by sea, according to sea-borne commodity data group Vortexa .
China also began stockpiling crude oil in October as imports recovered.
According to Hussain, “China does have some spare refinery capacity it could utilise”.
“But given that petrol and diesel inventories appear to be low in China, any increase in refined output may be used to replenish reserves rather than for export, which would keep global fuel supply constrained,” he said.
“In any case, the return of refined output from the Middle East will be key to lowering global fuel prices,” he added.

The British prime minister Andy Burnham said his deal with the European Union will add up to £17bn a year to the British economy as he paved the way for even closer ties to Brussels. Burnham said it was a “good day for Britain and a good day for Europe”, as he met EU chiefs in Brussels to announce a package covering food and agriculture exports, emissions trading, and a youth experience scheme which could open the doors for 100,000 young Europeans to temporarily work in the UK, with Britons able to do the same on the continent.
Burnham ‌said Friday’s deal was “probably the limit” of what could be done before the next national election due by mid-2029 , but he envisaged an informal conversation in about a year ‌with the EU about what could be achieved next.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she welcomed Burnham’s willingness to have a broad debate about future relations with the EU. “We are open for brainstorming, and we welcome this brainstorming, so count on us,” she said.
At the summit, postponed from July after the resignation of Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer, ‌the two sides addressed some of the Brexit losses with a package of agreements. The most significant allows cross-border trade in animals, plants and related products, such as sausages or seeds, without the certificates and controls currently required. Britain has estimated this could add up to £5.1bn per year to its economy.
A further agreement will link the emissions trading systems of Britain and the EU, which would exempt British and EU goods, such as steel, from each other’s border carbon levies. Each side is also set to allow 100,000 young people a year in to work or study for three years.
However, one potential dampener emerged as the 27-nation bloc and London jostled over linking ultimate implementation of the new deals to Britain agreeing to cut university fees for EU students. Britain ⁠prefers to offer only “significantly reduced” fees, and the aim is to resolve the issue within six months.
Retailers and manufacturers have welcomed Andy Burnham’s new trade deal with the European Union as a “big win” but warned they need “clear and early” guidance from government to aid the transition, Press Association reported. The chief executive of the British Retail Consortium (BRC) called the SPS deal a “big win” for UK retailers but warned that businesses need “at least 18 months” to transition to the new arrangements.
Nigel Farage, the veteran anti-EU campaigner and leader of the Reform UK party, said the deal “was about the first steps, incrementally, to taking us back into membership of the European Union,” and again predicted an early election next year. Farage told reporters he would campaign to preserve Brexit. “I am ready for this fight,” he said.
Meanwhile, Denmark’s foreign minister on Friday said Moscow’s defence attache in Copenhagen would be expelled after Russia was suspected of being behind an attempted assassination of a Ukrainian rapper. “We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the ministry of foreign affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attache from Denmark” within seven days, Lars Lokke Rasmussen told a news conference.
